input:
The results reported here relate to a shell-and-tube heat exchanger installed in a refinery preheat train, where its duty is to heat propylene glycol. The exchanger operates at a duty of 1377 kW. On the hot side, the stream enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C, while on the cold side the stream enters at 25 °C and leaves at 50 °C. Working from these terminal temperatures, the temperature difference at the hot end is 130 K and at the cold end is 105 K, giving a log-mean temperature difference of 117.1 K. With an installed area of 40.2 m2, the corresponding overall heat-transfer coefficient works out at 293 W m-2 K-1.

This overall coefficient is best understood as a measure of the performance of the exchanger as actually installed, referred to the installed area. It lumps together the resistances of the two fluid films, the resistance of the tube wall, and the resistance due to any fouling that had built up over the course of the run, and it provides the natural starting point for any future rerating exercise or for checking the unit against a revised duty. It is also worth noting that, because the two terminal differences differ considerably from one another, the log-mean value lies well below the hot-end figure, so that anyone sizing an exchanger on the hot-end difference alone would overestimate the effective driving force and end up with too little surface.

As far as fouling is concerned, the assessment rests on a single 90-day run, and it must be emphasised that no cleaning cycle has yet been completed. The reported coefficient accordingly characterises the exchanger over that one run only, and the available data say nothing about the extent to which performance recovers on cleaning, the rate at which fouling re-establishes itself afterwards, or whether the fouling eventually levels off.
target:
A shell-and-tube exchanger in a refinery preheat train heats propylene glycol. The duty is 1377 kW. The hot stream enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C; the cold stream enters at 25 °C and leaves at 50 °C. The terminal temperature differences are 130 K at the hot end and 105 K at the cold end, and the log-mean temperature difference is 117.1 K. On the installed area of 40.2 m2, the overall coefficient is 293 W m-2 K-1.

The coefficient is the installed performance, stated on the installed area. It folds the two film resistances, the tube wall, and whatever fouling had accumulated during the run into a single figure, and it is the figure from which a rerating of the same exchanger, or a check of the exchanger against a changed duty, would start. The duty and the four terminal temperatures fix that figure jointly; no one of them carries it alone. Because the terminal differences are wide apart, the log-mean difference sits well below the hot-end difference; a sizing checked against the hot-end difference alone would overstate the driving force along much of the exchanger and undersize the surface.

Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has been completed. The coefficient therefore describes the exchanger over that one run, from its condition at the start of the run to its condition at the end. The run does not show how far the coefficient recovers when the exchanger is cleaned, how quickly it falls again afterwards, or whether the fouling approaches a plateau. A cleaning interval and a long-run performance figure cannot be read from a single run; the measurement that would settle the fouling behaviour is a further run with a completed cleaning cycle inside it.
